summary: This clipped page is the 'Basic Recipes' section (3) of the picamera release-1.13 documentation, showing Python scripts for capturing images and recording video with the Raspberry Pi camera. It covers capturing to files, streams, PIL images, resized and consistent images, timelapse, low-light capture, network streaming, and video recording to files, streams, circular buffers and networks. The page is truncated just as it begins section 3.14 on overlaying images on the preview.
one_line: Python recipes from the picamera 1.13 docs for capturing images and recording video on a Raspberry Pi camera.
key_facts: The picamera basic recipes are section 3 of the release-1.13 documentation.
Warning: scripts should not be named picamera.py because that name clashes with the picamera module when Python imports it.
Capturing to a file example sets camera.resolution to (1024, 768) and calls camera.capture('foo.jpg') after a two-second warm-up sleep.
When capturing to a stream, picamera calls flush() on the object before capture returns but does not close it.
Capturing resized images uses the resize parameter, for example camera.capture('foo.jpg', resize=(320, 240)), so the GPU does the resizing.
To fix exposure, set shutter_speed, optionally set iso, let analog_gain and digital_gain settle, then set exposure_mode to 'off'; to fix white balance set awb_mode to 'off' and set awb_gains.
Rule of thumb in the recipe: ISO 100 and 200 are reasonable for daytime, while 400 and 800 are better for low light.
Capturing in low light uses a 6 second exposure, the maximum for the V1 camera module, while the V2 camera module can manage 10 second exposures.
The rolling shutter of the Pi camera module can distort moving subjects, and longer exposure times exaggerate this effect.
The network capture protocol sends the image length as a 32-bit little-endian integer, followed by the image bytes, and a length of 0 closes the connection.
Recording video to a stream sets quality=23; quality ranges from 1 (highest) to 40 (lowest), with 20 to 25 typical, and bitrate defaults to 17000000 with a maximum of 25000000.
The split_recording() method splits files only at a key-frame, so each file in the 10-file example is approximately 5 seconds long.
record_sequence() was introduced in picamera version 1.3.
PiCameraCircularIO was added in version 1.0 and copy_to() was added in version 1.11; the circular buffer example keeps 20 seconds of video.
VLC or mplayer will not work for playback on a Pi because neither can use the GPU for decoding, so playback must run on a faster machine.

entities.name: picamera
entities.role: Python library for controlling the Raspberry Pi camera, whose release-1.13 documentation contains these recipes

entities.name: PiCamera
entities.role: Main class used in the recipes to control the camera, with capture(), start_recording() and related methods

entities.name: PiCameraCircularIO
entities.role: Ring-buffer in-memory stream class for video recording, used to keep the last n seconds of video

entities.name: BytesIO
entities.role: Python in-memory stream class used as a capture or recording output in several recipes

entities.name: PIL
entities.role: Python Imaging Library used to open captured images as Image objects and verify them

entities.name: VLC
entities.role: Media player used by the network server recipe to display the H.264 stream, and noted as unsuitable for playback on a Pi

entities.name: mplayer
entities.role: Alternative media player for the network stream server recipe, also unsuitable for playback on a Pi

entities.name: raspivid
entities.role: Raspberry Pi camera executable that can be combined with netcat to stream video

entities.name: netcat
entities.role: Network utility used with raspivid and VLC as a simpler alternative streaming setup on Linux

entities.name: Raspberry Pi camera V1 module
entities.role: Camera module whose maximum exposure is 6 seconds

entities.name: Raspberry Pi camera V2 module
entities.role: Camera module that can manage 10 second exposures
